claims.text: GitHub's records give the Anthropic commit, authored by Thomas Steinke, at 20:04:44 UTC on 23 November. It was merged as PR #51 at 21:43:48 UTC [^6].
OpenAI's commit `e07100d`, "Add VP != VNP manuscript and Lean.", carries an author time of 01:14:20 UTC on 24 November.
The commit touched 3,163 files and added 442,736 lines [^18].
That difference explains why the press variously reported "four" and "five" hours [^45].
OpenAI's history file has one line on precedence: "VP and VNP are different. This result was obtained on November 6, 2026" [^10].
The paper's own date field is empty [^16].
Six weeks earlier, OpenAI's README had said it would "defer to the math community completely on matters of credit, precedence, and concurrent work" [^9].
Andrew Curran, who first flagged both uploads on X, reported that neither lab issued a blog post or announcement [^40,41].
The ETH refutations followed the same pattern a month earlier, with OpenAI uploading first that time, and nobody has suggested either lab copied the other [^7,10].
The permanent is VNP-complete over every field of characteristic other than two.
Bürgisser's 2024 survey notes that nobody knew how to prove even n² log n for the n×n permanent [^20].
Limaye, Srinivasan and Tavenas proved superpolynomial lower bounds for constant-depth circuits in 2021, and won a FOCS best paper award for it [^22].
Forbes extended that result to every field at CCC 2024 [^23].
A depth-3 bound of exp(ω(√d·log^(3/2) d)) for the permanent would already imply general superpolynomial lower bounds [^24], and LST-strength bounds sit well below that bar.
Fortnow said exactly this: "VP ≠ VNP does not imply this Boolean separation" [^35].
The border conjectures are known to be stronger than Valiant's own, though nobody knows by how much [^2,25].
The README sets out the trust model plainly: "Lean checks the proofs, but no machine checks that this file says what is claimed" [^1].
It points to Appendix Q of the paper, Table 3, as the map between paper and Lean statements and the list of where they differ [^1].

Then, over every field of characteristic p and for every m ≥ m₀, every circuit for the Hamiltonian cycle polynomial, and every circuit for the permanent when p ≠ 2, has more than m^(c·(log₂ m)^(1/3)) gates [^2].
VP is defined as families with variable count, total degree and circuit size all at most n^a + a. VNP is defined as Boolean sums of a VP family over r(n) auxiliary bits [^2].
**Vacuity**: `Beyond` uses `Real.logb 2 m`, and Mathlib returns junk value 0 for arguments 0, 1 and −1 [^49].

Comparator runs with an empty `definition_names` list, so the solver could not supply its own definitions [^3]. Comparator's README warns that challenges with such holes "can be gamed without additional oversight" [^27].
`comparator.json` lists five targets: `mainTheorem`, `mainTheoremApprox`, `separation`, `separationClosure` and a fifth, `permanent_over_real`, which the README does not mention [^3].
Each target is discharged by citing a theorem in the `Paper/` tree, so all the mathematics lives in untrusted files that only the kernels check [^4].

CI runs `lake build`, fails on any `sorry` outside `Challenge.lean`, forces `enable_nanoda=true`, and passes only on the exact line "Your solution is okay!". The workflow ran and passed on PR #51 before merge [^5].
The toolchain is Lean v4.33.1 [^8], newer than the July kernel-soundness fixes discussed in Section 6.

A secondary reading of Appendix Q reports that four supporting results, including the program constructions that the main theorem's "contracting" branch needs, are checked only in Lean and not written out in the paper [^43].
OpenAI's challenge file defines `Computes` with binary gates `a + b`, `a − b` or `a * b`. Inputs and field constants are free and not counted [^11].
OpenAI's 25 November hierarchy challenge, `strict_inclusions`, does state `VP F ⊂ VNP F` explicitly [^14].
`VPVNP.json` names one theorem, permits the three standard axioms, and sets `enable_nanoda: false`, so only Lean's own kernel checks the proof [^12].

The Hamiltonian-cycle and permanent bounds do exist, as `corollary12` in `Separation.lean`: for every exponent C and characteristic q, eventually m^C < circuitSize(HC_m), and the same for the permanent if q ≠ 2 [^13].
Theorem 1.1 of the manuscript reads: "Over every field, border circuits for f_n require exp(Ω((log n)^(5/4))) gates" [^16].
The Lean's `separation_lower_bound` says only that for every C ≥ 1 there is an N beyond which n^C < circuitSize. That is exact circuits, with no rate [^13].
The Hamiltonian-cycle paper claims exp(c·(log N)²/(log log N)²) gates over any field, but its README says the Lean proves "eventual superpolynomial exact circuit lower bounds" [^17].
The family-379 scope document lists seven items that remain unformalized, among them "the paper's explicit n^Ω((log n)^(1/12)) lower bound for the n×n grid" [^15].
It also describes the whole repository as "raw research data, rather than polished academic papers", with about 42% of top-line results formalized [^9].

In the other direction, OpenAI had already gone through a full public correction cycle before this release: on 7 October it withdrew three manuscripts because "a sign error invalidates a stabilization-trace cancellation argument" [^10].
With an external kernel enabled, the trust assumption weakens to "at least one of the Lean kernel or the `external_kernels` is correct" [^27].
The Lean reference manual draws the line plainly: "Lean can establish that a statement has been proven, but not whether it is the intended statement" [^28].
On 22 July, Lean 4.32.1 fixed a kernel bug that allowed proving `False`, though the recommended Comparator workflow was "not affected" [^44].
Six days later, 4.32.2 fixed a second bug in the handling of nested inductive types with phantom parameters. The release notes say: "The bug can be exploited even when using `comparator`" [^29].
nanoda did not share that bug, but Ramana Kumar showed one proof term could combine it with a separate nanoda flaw [^29].

The trigger, according to the oss-security advisory, was a published "Lean disproof of Collatz" that both kernels had accepted, which led to the conclusion that "independently rechecking Lean declarations was not sufficient against this particular implementation flaw" [^30].
Anthropic pins a nanoda build from a maintained fork and requires it to agree [^5].

Buzzard's 12 November audit of OpenAI's earlier release found that "around 38" of roughly 290 Lean-backed papers have Lean code that "does not even state, let alone prove, the main theorem of the paper" [^32].
DeepMind's Formal Conjectures project reports that 291 misformalizations have been fixed across 7,559 Lean statements.
Separately, a NeurIPS 2025 audit of the miniF2F benchmark found "discrepancies between the formal and informal statements for more than half of the problems" [^34].
Lance Fortnow wrote on X that he "ran this through Claude and Gemini and both checked the formalization, though didn't process the Lean proof", and called the result "likely correct" [^38].
His blog post the same day called it "for now, the most important computational complexity result of the year" [^35].
Scott Aaronson wrote that the Lean certifies correctness "to a level considerably beyond what we'd normally demand". He also invited experts to raise "any real technical issue" [^36].
Gil Kalai wrote that he is "overwhelmed" and "quite confused about the nature and speed of events" [^37].
Its own notes say the only change to `Statement.lean` is notational, which re-validates the proof, not the meaning of the statement [^46].
He adds that on the algebraic relativization barrier, "I don't know how to tell it yet" [^36].

Fortnow says Anthropic's proof "uses a variant of Strassen's asymptotic spectrum to split into two cases, one handled by a rank argument and the other by a diagonalization", with "essentially no algebraic geometry" [^35].
Anthropic's own Lean docstrings describe the same two-way case split, which the proof never decides [^50].
OpenAI credits "an unnamed internal OpenAI model" and says the project used about 4,000 posed problems and about three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result [^1,9].
**Maintenance.** OpenAI says two 24 November preprints "subsume" the 23 November paper, which "remains available unchanged" [^10].
Public scrutiny is already intense: the Hacker News thread on Anthropic's release had 366 points and 333 comments when ARA read it, though it mostly debated what the result means for P vs NP [^39].
Aaronson notes the two proofs "look similar" [^36].
